rvt.export.help: The IFC export settings that open best here
rvt.preview.what.typed: Lab preview: BimCraft can try to read the model in this project (saved in {release}) with the open-source rvt library. Where it can read them, walls, floors, roofs, columns, stairs and rooms come in with their shapes, and doors, windows and furniture as boxes; on some projects it reads much less. Most parameters are not read. Nothing is uploaded. Check it against an IFC export before you rely on it.
rvt.preview.what.boxes: Lab preview: BimCraft can try to read the model in this project (saved in {release}) with the open-source rvt library. For this release it reads walls with their shapes and most other elements only as boxes. Nothing is uploaded. Check it against an IFC export before you rely on it.
rvt.preview.what.experimental: Lab preview: BimCraft can try to read the model in this project (saved in {release}) with the open-source rvt library. Its support for this release is experimental: expect missing elements and boxes. Nothing is uploaded. Check it against an IFC export before you rely on it.

frame.ui.aid: An analysis aid, not a code check: forces, reactions and deflections of the members as modeled, by first-order linear analysis. It checks no design code. eg49.u.title: Uneven absorption (box room)
eg49.u.intro: Sabine and Eyring assume every surface absorbs alike. When one surface does most of the absorbing (a carpet under a hard ceiling), they read too short. Fitzroy and Arau-Puchades take the three pairs of opposite surfaces separately. Type the room as a box and pick its finishes.
eg49.u.uneven: The three pairs of surfaces absorb very differently here. Trust Fitzroy or Arau-Puchades over Sabine, and expect the real room to sit between them.
eg49.u.fs: Below about {fs} Hz this room has separate standing waves, not an even sound field (Schroeder frequency from a reverberation time of {t} s). The reverberation figures above do not describe those low bands.
eg49.u.modes.note: The lowest modes of a rigid empty box (axial, tangential and oblique, written as the three mode numbers). The smallest gap between two modes below 120 Hz is {gap} Hz; modes that sit close together make a boomy note. A design aid, not a measurement.
